name: Cibo & Ristorante
desc: Food, drinks and surviving the bill

vocabulary.note: Bread arrives unasked — and often with “il coperto”, a small cover charge. Check the menu, not the vibes.
Ordering water: “naturale” (still) or “frizzante” (sparkling). Tap water isn't a thing — that's “acqua del rubinetto”, and brace yourself.
“Un caffè” means espresso. If you want the big watery thing, ask for “un caffè americano” and endure the look you'll get.
A breakfast drink ONLY. Order one after lunch and the barista will still serve it — while quietly filing you under “tourist” forever.

vocabulary.ex: La pasta fatta in casa è la migliore.

vocabulary.note: Ananas sulla pizza: technically legal, morally contested. Your nonna's opinion is stronger than any law.
Asking for parmigiano on a fish pasta is considered a small act of war. Don't.
Rosso o bianco? House wine (“della casa”) is often the honest choice, and cheap.
Order “un cono” (cone) or “una coppetta” (cup). If it's florescent green pistachio, run — real pistachio is dull beige and delicious.
Say it loudly enough and someone will eventually come. Splitting the bill exists, but expect the waiter's quiet judgement.
To call them: “scusi!” works. Snapping your fingers does too — if you want to become the village's main character.
Italian breakfast is sweet: cappuccino + cornetto. Eggs at 8am will get you looks of pure anthropological curiosity.

vocabulary.ex: Una pasta al pomodoro, per favore.
vocabulary.exEn: A pasta with tomato sauce, please.
vocabulary.note: Pomodoro = pomo d'oro, 'golden apple'. The things etymology gives you.
On Christmas Eve, fish is mandatory — see la vigilia in Feste.
Verdura is singular in everyday Italian — 'le verdure' exists but the market says verdura.
One word, two jobs: the dessert course and the sweet taste. Il dolce far niente is neither, but it's the best one.
Crudo = the cured parma-style one, cotto = boiled sandwich ham. Ordering the wrong one is a rite of passage.

vocabulary.ex: Una caprese con mozzarella di bufala.
vocabulary.note: Di bufala vs normale: Italians have opinions. Strong, loud ones.

vocabulary.exEn: We dress the salad with olive oil.
vocabulary.note: At the table just say 'l'olio' — nobody drizzles anything else on their pinzimonio.

vocabulary.ex: Un po' di parmigiano sulla pasta?
vocabulary.exEn: A bit of parmesan on the pasta?
vocabulary.note: Real deal: Parmigiano Reggiano. 'Grana' is the cheaper cousin — fine, but be honest about it.

vocabulary.ex: Un caffè da portare via, grazie.
vocabulary.note: 'Da asporto' is understood but sounds like a supermarket. Humans say da portare via.

vocabulary.ex: Il piatto del giorno è la carbonara.
vocabulary.note: A proper meal goes primo, secondo, contorno, dolce. Asking for everything at once marks you as a tourist.
Italians HAVE hunger, they don't BE it: ho fame, hai fame. Same trick with thirst: ho sete.

vocabulary.exEn: Are you thirsty? I'll get you a water.
